CausalChain: Hypoxia in HCC -> HIF activation -> Upregulation of glycolytic enzymes and lactate transporters (MCT1 and MCT4) -> Increased lactate production and export -> Extracellular lactate accumulation leads to acidification and engagement of receptors (e.g., GPR81) -> Upregulation of PD-L1 and suppression of NK/CD8+ T cell function -> Creation of an immunosuppressive TME -> Drug resistance to TKIs and ICIs
Hypothesis: In hypoxic HCC, a dual intervention that combines selective inhibition of both MCT1 and MCT4 lactate transporters with precise modulation of the HIF pathway—delivered via nanotechnology-enhanced drug carriers and potentially optimized by CRISPR-based gene editing—will reduce extracellular lactate accumulation, thereby mitigating acidification and GPR81 receptor activation. This will lead to downregulation of PD-L1 and restoration of NK and CD8+ T cell cytotoxic functions, ultimately sensitizing tumors to immune checkpoint inhibitors and tyrosine kinase inhibitors and overcoming drug resistance.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by hypoxic regions that induce a cascade of metabolic and immunosuppressive alterations leading to drug resistance. The original concept focused on inhibiting MCT4-mediated lactate export to reverse lactate-induced immunosuppression. However, recent evidence indicates that MCT1 is the primary mediator of lactate export in HCC and that broad modulation of the HIF pathway can reshape the immune microenvironment. Here, we propose a revised hypothesis in which a dual-targeting strategy—combining selective inhibition of both MCT1 and MCT4 transporters with precise HIF pathway modulation using advanced nanotechnology-based drug delivery and gene editing tools—is employed to reduce extracellular lactate accumulation. This reduction alleviates acidification and GPR81 receptor engagement, thereby downregulating PD-L1 expression and restoring the cytotoxic functions of NK and CD8+ T cells. We hypothesize that by concurrently attenuating lactate export and HIF-driven metabolic reprogramming, tumors will be sensitized to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) and tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), ultimately overcoming drug resistance in HCC.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed that inhibiting MCT4 alone in hypoxic HCC would reduce lactate-induced immunosuppression. The revised hypothesis expands this approach by incorporating: (1) a dual targeting strategy to inhibit both MCT1 and MCT4, acknowledging that MCT1 is a key mediator of lactate export in HCC; (2) direct modulation of the HIF pathway to influence a broader range of hypoxia-induced metabolic adaptations; and (3) the use of modern technologies such as nanotechnology-based delivery systems and CRISPR for precise targeting. Each of these modifications directly addresses and refines the original causal chain steps—from hypoxia-induced HIF activation and lactate production, through extracellular lactate accumulation and immunosuppressive receptor engagement, to PD-L1 upregulation and immune cell suppression—thus enhancing both the mechanistic insight and practical implementability of the therapeutic strategy.
